summary.text: Climate classification sorts the world's climates into similar groups, an idea that began with climes defined in Ancient Greece by a location's latitude.
Modern methods are either genetic, built on the causes of climate, or empiric, built on its effects, such as plant hardiness or links to certain biomes.
The simplest approach labels air masses with letters for moisture, source-region temperature and stability, and all schemes draw sharper borders than nature has.

paragraphs.heading: What climate classification does
paragraphs.text: Climate classification groups the world's climates into a set of zones. There is more than one way to sort climates into similar types. The idea is old: in Ancient Greece, climes described the weather a place had according to its latitude. Since climate strongly shapes the life in a region, a climate scheme can line up closely with a scheme of biomes.

paragraphs.heading: Causes or effects
paragraphs.text: Modern methods fall into two broad families. Genetic methods look at what causes a climate, while empiric methods look at what a climate does. A genetic scheme might count how often different types of air mass pass over a place, or note where it sits within passing weather systems. An empiric scheme might draw zones from plant hardiness, from evapotranspiration, or from links to particular biomes, as the Köppen scheme does.

paragraphs.heading: Labelling air masses
paragraphs.text: The simplest approach classifies air masses, and the Bergeron system is the most widely accepted version. It gives each air mass three letters. The first tells moisture: c for continental, dry air, and m for maritime, moist air. The second tells the temperature of the air's source region, such as T for tropical or P for polar. The third describes stability: k if the air is colder than the ground beneath it, and w if it is warmer.

paragraphs.heading: From forecasts to climates
paragraphs.text: Air mass identification was first used for weather forecasting in the 1950s. In 1973 climatologists began building synoptic climatologies on the same idea. The Spatial Synoptic Classification, or SSC, grew out of Bergeron's scheme. It has six types: Dry Polar, Dry Moderate, Dry Tropical, Moist Polar, Moist Moderate and Moist Tropical, each roughly matching one or more of the older air mass labels.

paragraphs.heading: The Köppen scheme
paragraphs.text: The most used scheme of all, first developed in 1884, is Köppen's, an empiric one. It relies on monthly averages of temperature and precipitation. Its common form has five main types, A to E: tropical, dry, mild mid-latitude, cold mid-latitude and polar. A tropical place, for example, is one where even the coolest month averages above 18 °C (64.4 °F).

paragraphs.heading: A built-in limitation
paragraphs.text: A weakness these schemes often share is that they draw clear lines between zones. Real climates more often change gradually from one place to the next.
